title: ITV’s Zandland Doc ‘Inside Iran: War & Revolution’ Goes Undercover During Anti-Regime Protests & Conflict With The U.S.
full_text: Skip to main content By Stewart Clarke Stewart Clarke More Stories By Stewart ProSiebenSat.1 Ad Sales Dented By Weak TV Market & Rivals’ World Cup Rights Catherine Zeta-Jones Takes On The Seven Demons In Revenge Thriller ‘Kill Jackie’ BritBox & BBC’s Poirot Origin Series ‘Hercule’ Reveals Cast View All August 6, 2026 4:11am Inside Iran: War & Revolution ITV, Zandland EXCLUSIVE: ITV has greenlit Inside Iran : War & Revolution . The one-off doc goes undercover and inside Iran, with testimony from journalists and civilians during the 2025-2026 protests and, more recently, the conflict with the U.S. The film comes from UK-based doc studio Zandland . It marks another ITV-Zandland project following their BAFTA-nominated film Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s Army . Inside Iran: War & Revolution is told from the perspective of an anonymous Iranian journalist. It has access to people living inside Iran and under its authoritarian regime. The doc chronicles the struggles and suffering of protestors in the uprising and shows the brutal crackdown by the authorities, including footage from the mass protests, and inside the hospitals where the injured were being treated and also faced arrest. It goes on to give an inside-Iran account of the hostilities with the U.S. Related Stories News ITV Studios Bosses Bullish Despite U.S. & International Declines As 'Love Island' & 'The Gentlemen' Maker Prepares To Go Independent News ITV Reveals Early Share Buyback Of $140M Before Sky Deal Completes As Broadcaster Unveils First Set Of Results Since Confirming The Deal Capturing footage from inside Iran is perilous. The film spells out the risks the contributors took with an on-screen graphic that reads: “Almost all of the footage in this film was filmed inside Iran by citizens taking significant personal risks.” Given the risk of punishment or even execution, some contributions are anonymized or voices altered. Watch on Deadline Zandland is run by British-Iranian filmmaker Ben Zand . Based in London and Liverpool, the doc studio has harnessed YouTube and digital distribution , as well as working with traditional broadcasters. Zand directed Inside Iran: War & Revolution . “What this film captures is an impossible situation, and the full range of what it does to the people living through it,” Zand said. “Our contributors describe grief, fury, hope and heartbreak, often side by side, and rarely in the ways outside observers might expect. As a British-Iranian this is deeply personal to me, but the film belongs to the people inside Iran who risked everything to share their reality.” ITV’s Controller of Current Affairs, Tom Giles, commissioned Breaking Ranks: Inside Israel’s Army and also greenlit Inside Iran: War & Revolution . “This is a powerful and significant piece of work by people who have taken great risks to film and bear witness to events which have commanded the world’s attention all year, and which they themselves have directly experienced,” he said. “These are filmed voices we rarely hear from inside Iran: urgent, passionate, fearful and inspiring.” The film bows on ITV1 and streaming service ITVX on August 9. Maya Rostowska is the Producer, and Josh Reynolds and Ben Zand are the Executive Producers. title: Warner Bros. Discovery Stumbles In Q2 As ‘Supergirl,’ Lack Of NBA Drag Down Results
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Sinclair CEO Chris Ripley “Couldn’t Be Happier” About Expected FCC Repeal Of Federal Ownership Cap Disney Sells Out Super Bowl Ad Inventory, Wraps Upfront Sales Process ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Triumph “Bodes Well” For ‘Avengers: Doomsday’, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro Says View All August 6, 2026 4:10am An aerial view of the Warner Bros. studio lot in Burbank, CA Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Warner Bros. Discovery fell short of Wall Street expectations in the second quarter, as Supergirl and the lack of the NBA dragged total revenue down 11% to $8.7 billion. Analysts had projected $9.2 billion in revenue. Diluted earnings per share of 6 cents topped estimates of a loss of 10 cents a share. The company reported the quarterly financials with its $110 billion merger with Paramount in legal limbo. The attorneys general of 12 states, as well as the Writers Guild of America, have filed a lawsuit seeking to block the deal on antitrust grounds. A trial has been scheduled for March 2027. Streaming proved a bright spot, with total revenue up 10% to $3.1B and EBITDA jumping 75% to $512 million. Flagship streamer HBO Max, which has recently expanded to key international territories, was paced by titles like Euphoria , House of the Dragon , Hacks and The Pitt . Related Stories Legal Judge Dismisses Consumer Lawsuit Challenging Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery Merger News Regal Cinemas CEO Eduardo Acuna Champions Paramount-WBD Merger, Says Antitrust Trial "Creates More Uncertainty And Distraction" The studio division faced tough comparisons with the year-ago period, which featured hits like A Minecraft Movie , Sinners , and Final Destination Bloodlines . Revenue tumbled 39% to $2.3 billion and EBITDA plummeted 89% to $96 million. Supergirl grossed just $126 million worldwide, the lowest for any DC release since Catwoman in 2004. Watch on Deadline Total advertising revenue plunged 22% from the year-ago period to settle at $1.7 billion. The main culprit was the absence of the NBA. After nearly 40 years of broadcasting the league’s games, WBD did not reach a deal to extend its rights, with NBCUniversal taking its place as a primary partner. The ad story marred the quarterly performance of the Global Linear Networks division, whose revenue slid 17% to $3.99 billion. Adjusted EBITDA was off 4% to $1.4 billion. The quarterly numbers followed Tuesday’s earnings report from Paramount, which featured some updated comments about the WBD merger. full_text: × Skip to main content By Etan Vlessing Plus Icon Etan Vlessing Canada Bureau Chief View All August 6, 2026 4:02am Versant CEO Mark Lazarus Photo by Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images for Semafor World Econom Versant , the cable TV-focused spinoff from NBCUniversal that runs CNBC , MS NOW , USA, Golf Channel and other assets, reported lower second earnings on lower revenue and public company costs from its Comcast separation. Now solo Versant reported revenue for the quarter to June 30 at $1.64 billion, down 3.8 percent from $1.7 billion in the same period of 2025. In that revenue mix, linear distribution was down 6.3 percent to $954 million, as Versant continues to rely on a declining pay TV business. Advertising revenue at $423 million was down just under 1 percent from the year-earlier period when ad revenue dropped 13 percent. Platforms revenue grew 0.8 percent to $212 million, and content licensing revenue was unchanged at $43 million. Discovery would like you to focus on its second quarter 2026 streaming revenue — up 9 percent to $3.1 billion — because the box office was ugly. Theatrical revenue dropped 46 percent from the comparable quarter last year as Supergirl and The Bride bombed. Making matters worse, their comps were to Q2 2025 hits A Minecraft Movie and Sinners . Discovery would record $9.21 billion in quarterly revenue. Another miss: WBD reported total revenues of $8.717 billion; net income was $100 million. And yet, Paramount Skydance still wants it. The process — and the drama — continues for David Ellison’s $111 billion takeover of WBD. There have been regular calls emanating from the U.S. and abroad to block the deal. It was originally supposed to be Netflix that bought the “WB” piece of “WBD,” but Ellison swooped in with an even bigger check and a promise to absorb the company in its entirety. A coalition of a dozen states are attempting to block Paramount/WBD; the case will go to trial in March 2027 . Meanwhile, beginning Oct. 1, 2026, Paramount Skydance must begin paying a ticking fee of $7 million per day to WBD shareholders. The ticking fee is only paid out if the deal closes. Ellison believes the opposition is politically motivated and centers on his potential oversight of CNN’s editorial content. He already controls CBS News, which has undergone many changes since Ellison’s Skydance merged with Paramount Global. “The issue is whether I can be trusted as a steward of Warner’s CNN. There has been speculation about my politics, my loyalties, my intentions,” he wrote in a recent New York Times op-ed . “Unfortunately, I can’t give anyone a view into my heart and mind, but I can share this: I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans; and when it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth.” There were no updates provided on the pending deal within Warner Bros. Discovery’s earnings report. THR

title: How Vicky McClure Became the Reigning Queen of the British Police Procedural
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 3:30am Vicky McClure is one of the U.K.'s best-known actors. Photographer: Billie Scheepers; Styling: Prue Fisher; Make-up: Justine Jenkins; Hair: Louis Byrne Vicky McClure wants to set the record straight. We’ve found a precious 40 minutes away from the hustle and bustle of press day for season four of ITV ‘s Trigger Point at London’s Soho Hotel. Tucked into the corner of one of its underground bars, McClure speaks to The Hollywood Reporter while her co-stars — Eric Shango, Natalie Simpson, Maanuv Thiara among them — dutifully pose for photos and laud the latest work of show creator Daniel Brierley. McClure, returning as the no-nonsense bomb disposal expert Lana Washington in another high-octane, watch-behind-your-hands instalment, is taking us through her early years at Nottingham’s Television Workshop, a Midlands-based film, TV, and theatre training school for kids from working-class backgrounds. She had initially eyed a career in professional dance and landed a place at the prestigious Italia Conti academy. But her family couldn’t afford the tuition. She stayed with the Television Workshop until the age of 21. Related Stories Movies Busan Film Festival to Honor Michelle Yeoh as Asian Filmmaker of the Year Business Soft Ad Market, World Cup Competition Hit Germany's ProSiebenSat.1 Results I halt the conversation early on to ask if what I’ve read online — that McClure was mentored at the Workshop by The Odyssey breakout Samantha Morton , a fellow Nottingham native — is true. The actress is quick to clarify: “That isn’t correct. Sam is a huge part of the Workshop, and my word, I mean, even now, the gigs that she’s in,” she says, alluding to the latest Christopher Nolan hit, wide-eyed with awe. “[But] we never crossed over. I actually didn’t know her while I was in the Workshop.” The pair would, later in their respective careers, meet at odd events. “You gravitate to each other if you’re both from Nottingham or the Workshop,” explains McClure, who was proudly born and raised in the English city (she has resisted the industry-induced pressure to relocate to the capital — a decision we’ll come to later). It was only when both of them were leading Dominic Savage’s I Am… series that McClure and Morton ended up “having a long chat on the phone.” They’ve stayed in touch, and McClure certainly calls her peer “an icon of the Workshop, and of the acting world.” But, contrary to what the internet purports, this friendship didn’t blossom until well beyond the Nottingham Television Workshop, which McClure remains a devoted patron of. And while Morton’s face currently graces thousands of cinema screens across the world, it is Vicky McClure who is known far and wide here in Britain. She has steadily risen through the ranks for two decades now to become one of the most prolific actors in the country, famed for her forthright characters and becoming, frankly, a legend of the U.K. police procedural ( Line of Duty , Broadchurch , to name a few). With Trigger Point continuing to pull in millions of viewers — season three’s seven-day consolidated average came in at 5.1m last year — and a hotly anticipated Line of Duty return imminent, McClure, now 43, enters a chapter of her career marked by prolificacy, freedom, and industry-wide reverence. Vicky McClure (center) in 2006’s ‘This Is England.’ IFC Films/Courtesy Everett Collection Her starring role aged 23 as Lol Jenkins in Shane Meadows’s 2006 film This Is England , and in the Channel 4 sequel mini-series This Is England ’86 , This Is England ’88 and This Is England ’90 from 2010 to 2015, is what she considers her long-awaited big break. “But I went straight back to the office,” McClure tells THR about her job at a house valuation company. “There’s just an illusion that once you’re in a film or you’re in something, that’s it. Onward you go,” she continues. “I’d train new people, then I sort of went into the HR department, looked after things like the vending machines, the post, a wide variety. I was even fire warden at one point, which I think has done me well for drifting into Lana,” she laughs. “That was my thing. I’d go off and do This Is England , and then I’d come back.” She worked at the business for eight years, and in that time, starred in a film directed by Madonna, Filth and Wisdom (2008). “We always think people care more than they do,” McClure says when asked what her office mates thought of the Madonna gig. “You know what I mean? They go, ‘Oh, amazing. That’s cool. Well, we’re having lunch.'” The reality is, while McClure was shooting with mega-stars, she was also getting told “no” a lot. “I learnt very quickly to stop telling people when I had an audition because nine times out of 10, I never got the job,” she admits. She recalls going up for roles in Peaky Blinders and Sarah Gavron’s 2015 Suffragette film. “That was one of those moments,” she says about feeling particularly heartbroken by the Suffragette casting, which eventually went to Carey Mulligan, Helena Bonham Carter, Anne-Marie Duff and Meryl Streep. “I wasn’t really that bothered about learning too much at school. I’d missed out on lots of history, so Jonny [Owen, McClure’s husband, also an actor and producer] sat down with me and we talked about the suffragette movement in great detail. I started getting really attached to this world and these characters.” Over time, she nailed the accent — “at the Workshop, it wasn’t like you trained to do accents, you just did them” — but eventually, nothing came of it. “They’re a bit naughty,” she says. “Sometimes casting directors can do that thing where they go, ‘So you’re available for those dates?’ Come on, guys. That’s basically a: ‘Let’s shake hands and roll the cameras!'” Still, on TV especially, McClure gradually made a name for herself with small roles in Five Daughters , The Body Farm and True Love . Then, in 2012, Jed Mercurio’s Line of Duty hit BBC Two. The series, about an anti-corruption unit inside a fictional police force, accrued a cult following around the world. Perhaps for the first time, McClure, as the driven, undaunted Detective Constable (later Sergeant and Inspector) Kate Fleming, was getting her flowers. “I don’t think I felt fame throughout This Is England ,” she ponders. “People were really respectful of that show, and it was such an ensemble piece that it didn’t belong to just one person. It was a really special show… [And] I think Line of Duty [is too]. It’s not a fluke because Jed’s writing is obviously impeccable, but it’s all down to the audience, and if they start tuning in and if they show [interest], then you’re in a good spot. But there’s every chance it can go [the other way], and shows do, don’t they?” says the veteran of British broadcast television, likely well acquainted with the graveyard of BBC and ITV shows haunting various streaming platforms. “No one watches them, and then a few years later, there’s this weird surge where everyone starts watching them again.” When the news of Line of Duty ‘s season seven broke last year, it certainly wasn’t a surprise to McClure. “We’d never closed the door,” says Mercurio’s star. “Me, Jed, [co-stars] Martin [Compston] and Aidy [Adrian Dunbar] meet up for a curry at least a couple of times a year. We’ve always had a sociable time when we make the show,” she continues, “and I think that comes across. We always said, ‘Oh, it’d be a shame if [season six] was the last one,’ because we felt like we had a really different experience [during] COVID… So then it was a case of: How are the stars going to align? We’ve all been lucky to get other gigs. Of course, Jed’s busy. He’s got to write it. We knew when he started to pick up his pen again…” she pauses, flashing a grin. (L-R) Martin Compston, Adrian Dunbar, Vicky McClure in ‘Line of Duty.’ Courtesy Everett Collection It is interesting, McClure adds, that Line of Duty is predominantly a cast of working-class people, “written by Jed, who grew up in a working-class family in Birmingham,” she says. “And it plays out on screen — you have accents and you have characters that are able to tap into certain flaws. Relationships were formed that are so long-lasting. Martin and Aidy are family now. I adore them both. So [hiring working-class talent] works. People need a bit more belief in those lives and characteristics.” McClure has been a champion of opening doors for working-class creatives her whole career. Her work with the Television Workshop is testament to that, though she isn’t content yet — by any means. “London should not be the center of the universe. For anything,” she says. “Don’t get me wrong, it’s an amazing city. But there is Nottingham, Birmingham, Manchester, Glasgow… The world’s a beautiful place, but with the industry in tow, it can’t all be London central. It has been and it still is, for so many years. And it’s just not serving anyone now.” When I put to her that there has been something of a production boom outside of the capital — in Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland — she maintains that while shoots are there, all of the really important get-togethers still happen in London. “It’s really naive of us to think that people can just afford that horrendous train fare or the petrol, or whatever it may be, [and] to just up and leave to get to that meeting. And I remember it was tricky for me. To get here and go, ‘I need to grab a sandwich and a cup of tea’ or something. It’s expensive.” McClure knows from first-hand experience that thousands of young actors will miss out on network-building because they can’t pay London rent: “It’s a very privileged space, a very privileged industry.” And even when the long-hoped-for acclaim arrives, the quote-unquote “fame” comes with unwanted side effects. “I don’t want to sit here and go, ‘It’s been a problem for me,'” concedes McClure, who says that staying in Nottingham has made showbiz a more liveable place — literally — for an actor of her calibre. “I like to do things here and there. When I get nice invitations, if I can make them, and it’s something I want to do, I’ll go, and the paps [paparazzi] will do what they’ll do. You can kind of control it, to a degree. You can choose to put yourself out there a bit more — and sometimes you need it. You need the promotion to help whatever business it is you’re trying to sell.” This is the more pragmatic side to McClure. With a BAFTA and a handful of wildly popular shows under her belt, you can’t deny it: She knows the ropes. “It’s a business and I’m in my mid-40s now,” she continues. “I’m a bit wiser, a bit longer in the tooth. I can see what things are, and you’re less naive. I’m not Hollywood. I feel Hollywood talking to The Hollywood Reporter ,” she says, smiling again, though admitting she’s never even been to L.A. (Tinseltown may yet come knocking — McClure’s next film, Kenneth Branagh’s The Last Disturbance of Madeline Hynde , sees her next to Jodie Comer, Patricia Arquette and Michael Sheen.) “I think when I’m on my deathbed,” she continues, “I won’t be worrying about my career.” What might McClure be more concerned with? Her charity work, for one — in 2019, she formed Our Dementia Choir following her late grandmother’s Alzheimer’s diagnosis. The organization was the subject of a BBC documentary, led by McClure, and over the years the group has performed in front of tens of thousands, including at Nottingham’s Splendour Festival. She also has a production company co-founded with her husband, Build Your Own Films, backed by All3Media and committed to nurturing projects “rich in subject matter, diversity and representation.” McClure in a first-look image of Lana Washington from season four of ‘Trigger Point.’ ITV1 Right now, however, it’s more Trigger Point on the telly for McClure. Releasing soon, the new season promises a deeper look into Lana’s trauma and, as you might have guessed, some pretty explosive drama. “There’s no joke to her job. It is life and death,” McClure says about returning to everyone’s favorite Expo. “We feel like we’ve seen it all in Trigger Point . Different types of scenarios.” She stops. Eye contact. “You haven’t seen it all.” She says this season’s writing team had a lot of fun concocting more dire situations for the Met Police bomb squad. “And we really own that. If there’s anyone that can go out with a bang, it’s Trigger Point . This is the bomb show.” She remembers reading a Times paper describing the series as “ Scooby-Doo on acid.” It was meant to be, according to McClure, a bit of a diss. She loved it. “It is Scooby-Doo on acid!” she beams. Most importantly, this Nottingham native is given the opportunity to take on the fearless Lana Washington once more, and it’s exactly where Vicky McClure wants to be. “I love it when she has one of them ‘fuck you’ moments. I always slip in a few more fucks than I probably should!” Catch McClure in the brand new series of Trigger Point , coming soon to ITV1 and STV. THR

title: Brian Cox, James D’Arcy Among First Guests on Rosie Fellner’s ‘Tea With Rosie’ Podcast (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 3:00am Rosie Fellner Tom Oxley Actor-producer Rosie Fellner ( The Uninvited , The Trip to Italy ) has launched a podcast, Tea With Rosie , and Succession star Brian Cox is among her first guests. Rosebud Pictures describes the project as Fellner “exploring life’s curveballs over Afternoon Tea,” with James D’Arcy ( Oppenheimer, Avengers: Endgame ), Eve ( Barbershop , The Talk ), Millie Brady ( The Last Kingdom , Surface ) and Shelley Conn ( Bridgerton , Gen V ) also set to feature on the show’s first season. “Like so many of us in the U.K., tea is a constant ritual in my life, bringing comfort, clarity, and — best of all — connection,” said Fellner to The Hollywood Reporter . “ Tea With Rosie came from a very simple place. I love people, I’m endlessly fascinated by their stories, and I’ve always believed the best conversations happen when you sit down with a good cup of tea and give someone the time to really talk.” Related Stories Movies 'Revolutionaries Never Die' Is a Cinematic Homage to Lebanese Filmmaking Pioneer Jocelyne Saab Movies Busan Film Festival to Honor Michelle Yeoh as Asian Filmmaker of the Year She continued about her experience in the industry: “I’ve spent years working in film, surrounded by extraordinary people, and I’ve realised the stories you remember are almost never the polished ones; they’re the strange turns, the near disasters, and the moments when someone took a chance and hoped for the best. The most interesting adventures of my life have usually started with an instinct, a slightly ridiculous idea, and absolutely no clue where it might lead. Tea With Rosie is about what happens when we follow the white rabbit, those moments when life takes an unexpected turn and you decide, for better or worse, to see where it leads.” Fellner began her career on the cult comedy series The Fast Show and would go on to appear in the likes of The Alan Clarke Diaries , My Hero , The Eustace Bros , The Line of Beauty and Disney+’s recently acclaimed A Small Light . In film, her credits include The Trip to Italy with Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, as well as The Face of an Angel , The Crew and Heist , starring Robert De Niro. She later founded Rosebud Pictures, an independent production company, with producing credits such as the SXSW-premiering The Uninvited , starring Pedro Pascal, Walton Goggins, Elizabeth Reaser, and Rufus Sewell, and Rabbit Trap , starring Dev Patel, which she executive produced ahead of its Sundance premiere in 2025. She is currently in post-production on the psychological thriller Trash TV . Her “whimsical, yet cheekily disarming questions” prompt a series of candid conversations where Tea With Rosie guests share personal reflections on their career, parenthood, success, failure, second chances and lessons learned along the way. The podcast will be available on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts this September, dropping weekly episodes. Tea With Rosie is sponsored by Mackenzie-Childs. THR

title: Isabella Rossellini Discusses “Empty Local Cinemas” and Why She Isn’t Leaving the U.S., for Now, Despite a “Very Bad” Political Situation
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 6, 2026 2:59am Isabella Rossellini at the Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival/Ti-Press On Wednesday evening, Italian-American actress, model and filmmaker Isabella Rossellini helped kick off the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival with star power, receiving the Swiss fest’s Excellence Award . On Thursday, the icon discussed her career and other insights during a public conversation as part of the festival program. In between anecdotes about her collaborations with famous directors and actors, things turned political for a moment when an audience member asked her about life in the U.S. and whether she ever considers moving for political reasons. The translation of the question and her response didn’t include mentions of U.S. President Donald Trump, but the query was widely understood as a reference to some creatives’ discussions of a potential move abroad due to Trump. “America is a continent,” Rossellini started off her response as the question had mentioned “America” rather than the U.S., querying the audience member: “Why do you live in Europe if there is a country you don’t like?” Related Stories Movies Isabella Rossellini and a Smiley Newcomer Charm Locarno as Refugee Adventure Drama Opens Fest Movies 'The Green Eyes' Is a Refugee Adventure Drama for Our Time (Exclusive Trailer) But she then seemed to focus on U.S. politics, saying: “The political situation is very bad, very hard. We’re thinking about going back. But I have a farm. I have sheep. I have hens. I have land.” That was a reference to her primary home, Mama Farm, a big organic farm that she founded in 2013 on Long Island. “So, should we abandon everything?” Rossellini continued. “We are going to stay, so far, and I hope that things will get better.” Rossellini on Thursday also received a broad question about changes and disruptions affecting the entertainment industry. Streaming, AI and other technologies bring “a lot of opportunities but also a crisis,” the icon offered. “Film festivals are crowded, but then local movie cinemas are empty.” Her comments about local cinemas come at a time, though, when the industry is breathing a sigh of relief, with 2026 currently on track to be the biggest domestic box office year since the COVID pandemic. But she concluded on an upbeat note, saying: “I’m optimistic. Creating art has always been difficult… And there are beautiful films being made with iPhones only.” How does Rossellini feel about acting in series? “I don’t like TV shows because they are so long,” she said, explaining she meant simply the amount of time they require, not any creative aspects. “I just want to be a guest star because I don’t want to stay away from home for eight months,” Rossellini shared. “That’s why I stopped doing theater.” In being honored on Locarno’s Piazza Grande on Wednesday evening, Rossellini recalled how her famous father Paolo and brother Renzo had previously received awards at Locarno, sharing: “To be on par with my father and my brother fills me with great emotion.” Her Thursday conversation was moderated by Olivier Père, the former artistic director of the Locarno festival and now executive director of ARTE France Cinéma and head of its cinema unit since 2012. He is also part of the jury for the international competition of Locarno79. THR

title: Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’
full_text: Aug 6, 2026 2:26am PT Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’ By Marta Balaga Plus Icon Marta Balaga Latest Isabella Rossellini Talks Lynch, ‘Green Porno’ and How Animals Became Her Favorite ‘Muses’: ‘They Fascinate Me’ 2 hours ago ‘Gagarine’ Directors Fanny Liatard and Jérémy Trouilh Talk ‘The Green Eyes’ as Kinology Announces First Sales: ‘Dreamers Know No Borders’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Locarno’s StepIn Focuses on ‘Power, People, Data and the Future of Film’: ‘The Counter-Algorithm Is a Human Being Who Gives a Damn’ (EXCLUSIVE) 1 week ago See All Credit: Edoardo Nerboni Isabella Rossellini has received the Excellence Award at Locarno. “The prize I’m receiving tonight is for excellence, which is something I haven’t heard very often,” she said during the opening ceremony. “I’m very proud of it and, above all, so moved because my father received this back in 1948 for his film ‘Germany, Year Zero.’ And then, four years ago, my brother Renzo [Rossellini], who was a great producer of Fellini and Scola. Being on par with my father and my brother fills me with so much emotion.” Related Stories Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets During her masterclass at the fest, Rossellini – who holds a master’s degree in Animal Behavior and Conservation – also opened up about her popular web series “Green Porno” and “Seduce Me,” about animal mating rituals. Popular on Variety “I know nothing about computers. I don’t speak that language, so I made these films the way I knew how: super low-tech. I watched a lot of [Georges] Méliès. It was a no-tech technique. Animals, to me, they fascinate me. I have a farm and when I decided to make films myself, they became my muses,” she said. She is now developing a new series of shorts about the evolution of domestic animals. “It’s called ‘The Survival of the Friendliest.’ We always focus on the survival of the fittest, but this one is so important.” She will play all the roles. But she would like to concentrate on directing more in the future. “I am just fascinated by biology and diversity. When someone says: ‘It’s against nature to be gay or trans’ — it’s not! I don’t sit down to write something political or poetic, but I discover that earthworms are hermaphrodites. I am just always so surprised. That’s my inspiration – not politics.” She can’t ignore the ongoing political situation in the U.S., however. “It’s difficult right now and we are thinking of going back, but I have sheep, chickens, I have land. Should I abandon everything? For now, I’m staying. I just hope things will improve,” she said, answering a question from the audience. “My first passion was animals. Even when I was a kid, I would take stray dogs and take them home.” Still, she had to follow her second passion first – for a while, she worked on her father’s films as a costume designer. When her mother, Ingrid Bergman, was offered a film in Rome, “A Matter of Time,” she ended up playing a small role in it, too. “Just to spend some time with my mum! I didn’t think I would become an actress.” Discouraged by early critics, she pursued modeling and journalism, too. “When you are criticized publicly, as it happened with ‘The Meadow,’ it’s really hard. Being successful in the fashion world really reassured me. I worked with Avedon, and he told me: ‘Models are like silent movie stars. You have no lines, but I shoot the emotion.’ I was asked to be in films, maybe because I was Ingrid Bergman’s daughter, and I said: ‘Why not’?” She recalled meeting David Lynch for the first time to discuss her role in “Blue Velvet,” released in 1986. “I met David at a restaurant. We were both there with members of the De Laurentis family, and we joined the tables. He said: ‘You look like Ingrid Bergman.’ They said: ‘You idiot, she is her daughter!’ When I got the script, there was a note: ‘Why don’t you read it and tell me if you want to play this character. I loved it, but it was so controversial. I asked him if I could rehearse the scenes to see if my interpretation matches his [vision]. He said: ‘You got it right.’” “David was not so famous back then, and he really showed his mysterious world there. The plot was not so important. Some hated it and some loved it.” Composer Angelo Badalamenti helped her as well. “It sounds like I sing very well, but that’s movie magic.” Later, she went on to work with Robert Zemeckis, David O. Russell, Taylor Hackford and James Gray on “Two Lovers.” Gray is also celebrated at Locarno this year. “He was very nice. Joaquin Phoenix was more difficult, because he followed method acting back then. I come from neorealist cinema, where you always hurry and worry about money – and James didn’t have any. And Joaquin, when there was a scene where he had to sleep, said: ‘I have to sleep for real.’ I was so worried.” she laughed. She also praised “magical” Alice Rohrwacher – she worked with her on “La Chimera” – and was nominated for an Academy Award as Best Supporting Actress for Edward Berger’s “Conclave.” “I never think about someone’s ‘style.’ I think about what I want to say.” “When I turned 42, Lancôme didn’t renew my contract because I was ‘too old’. They took me back 20 years later, but it was a difficult moment. I wasn’t working that much as an actor, either. It just stopped. I was told that middle-aged women had no audience. I started making my films and then things have changed – maybe our society has changed its opinion on middle-aged women. I overcame that moment thanks to my curiosity. I also have to credit Robert Redford, who told me: ‘You can be a director’.” Redford was the one who asked her to create something for Sundance Channel. She added: “The thing is, I did everything late. Maybe because my parents were so well-known? I became a model when I was 27 years old, 22 when I started acting, I earned my master’s degree when I was 55 and I became a director in my 50s. I would have liked to start everything earlier, because I’m always 10 years too late!” NBCU’s Peacock Limited-Ads Tier Launches on YouTube Primetime Channels Jesse Eisenberg on Why It Would Be ‘Silly’ to Leave U.S. Because of Trump, Says ‘The Debut’ Is ‘The Opposite of AI’ Following A24 DeepMind Partnership Peacock to Be Included in YouTube Premium Subscription Bundle Starting in 2027 Olivia Wilde’s ‘The Invite’ Nears $40 Million Globally, Becoming a Rare Hit Summer Comedy ‘Ponies’ Canceled After One Season at Peacock ‘Backrooms’ Extended Version Coming to Theaters With 15 Minutes of Bonus Footage Loading comments... Eight years in the making, “Concrete Land” follows one of the last Afro-Palestinian Bedouin families living on the outskirts of Amman, Jordan. As luxury villas encroach on the agricultural land they have long called home, the Najar family faces mounting pressure to abandon their traditional way of life. Forced to give up their animals and confronted with eviction, they struggle to preserve their identity while their 10-year-old daughter, Eman, navigates discrimination at school and dreams of a future that doesn’t require leaving her heritage behind. Their erasure is my erasure. I wasn’t a filmmaker before meeting the Najars. I believed their beauty was too precious to be lost, their knowledge too vital to be erased. title: ‘Revolutionaries Never Die’ Is a Cinematic Homage to Lebanese Filmmaking Pioneer Jocelyne Saab
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 6, 2026 2:00am 'Revolutionaries Never Die' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival In late Lebanese filmmaker and war reporter Jocelyne Saab’s 1982 film Beirut My City , she can be seen standing in front of her house after it was bombed and destroyed. Belgium-based Palestinian filmmaker Mohanad Yaqubi ( R21 AKA Restoring Solidarity , Off Frame AKA Revolution Until Victory ) can relate — his family’s house in Gaza was bombed in April 2024. It is just one connection between the two. Another is an invitation that Yaqubi received from the female pioneer to collaborate just two months before she died, which he didn’t answer at the time. So it’s perhaps fitting that Yaqubi decided to explore the work of Saab during her first decade of filmmaking, from 1973 to 1983. And he does so in his new film Revolutionaries Never Die , which will premiere in the Filmmakers of the Present competition program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival on Aug. 9. Related Stories Movies Busan Film Festival to Honor Michelle Yeoh as Asian Filmmaker of the Year Business Soft Ad Market, World Cup Competition Hit Germany's ProSiebenSat.1 Results Yaqubi, who is also the Palestine Film Institute’s public programmer and whose company Idioms Film produced Revolutionaries Never Die , describes the film, a cinematic letter to Saab, this way: “Jocelyne Saab’s film archive from 1973 to 1983 brought forward several questions about the striking resonance between her historical depictions and our contemporary realities five decades later, when no answers can ever be given.” Square Eyes is handling international sales. ‘Revolutionaries Never Die,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Locarno artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro, in an interview with THR , lauded the film as paying homage to “the legacy of the magnificent Lebanese filmmaker,” and Saab for documenting “with an uncanny eye for the future the onset of the Iranian revolution” and more. “She was this living memory of what was going on, and the film is basically about the work and the life of Jocelyne Saab as a living archive,” he concluded. Yaqubi never met Saab. Before diving into his new archive film, he wasn’t even too familiar with much of her work. “I knew a bit about her work, some of the famous films, like Letter From Beirut and others, before she passed away,” Yaqubi tells THR . “My work is really focused on this militant cinema period in the ‘60s and ‘70s. Her name always comes up, but I was more focused on what is considered Palestinian and on the topic of militant cinema itself. There was nothing much written about her. So, I really didn’t know much about her until we did a film program with the collective I work with and with the Courtisane Film Festival. The program was called ‘Out of the Shadows,’ and it was about five female filmmakers from the Arab world, with the others [being] Heiny Srour, Atteyat Al-Abnoudy, Selma Baccar and Assia Djebar. These are filmmakers from the Arab world, pioneers, politically committed, making films beside their male colleagues.” Yaqubi recalls wondering why Saab and her work, as well as others, weren’t more widely known and recognized. “The question is always: Why don’t we know about these things and these people?” he shares. “It’s also related to this society that is based on the male gaze at the end of the day, even when it comes to topics of liberation.” Mohanad Yaqubi Courtesy of Mohanad Yaqubi At first, his dive into Saab’s archive was “a restoration project,” he explains. “Mathilde Rouxel, who was her assistant in the last seven, eight years before she passed away, approached me, and because I had a film scanner in my office, we said, let’s do the scanning,” Yaqubi shares. “This is how I got to know her work.” And then, shared experiences became obvious. “The parallels started to show up after my house in Gaza was destroyed,” Yaqubi tells THR . “And I was invited by the Cinematek in Brussels to present this film, and it was three or four days after our house was destroyed in Gaza. And I saw this on the screen, and suddenly I couldn’t take it. And I thought, let me check out these parallels.” The filmmaker also felt he had to think about how to continue Saab’s work. “She made all these films and then somehow condensed all of her experience in one film, so for me the question was how do I continue that?” Yaqubi says. “It’s still only my third film. I’m working on cinema, but at the same time, I’m carrying this heavy feeling. What does it mean to be a committed filmmaker? It’s as if a decision has been made that I can’t make anything unless I’m committed to films for liberation, in a sense. But how do you do that? Where do you learn that? If you go to any film schools, they will not teach you these things. This is something that you have to explore and research. I feel that this film, even though it’s my third feature, is really my first film.” The question of whether he wanted to or could even continue making films weighed on Yaqubi amid the latest escalations in the Middle East. “I made a decision on how I’m going to continue making films,” he tells THR . “But after October 7 and these whole atrocities that happened, why do we make films? I teach my students about the Frankfurt School, [the group of philosophers, sociologists and other thinkers who created Critical Theory and analyzed Nazism and more]. They all talked about the genocide, the Holocaust, violence and all of those things and Western ideologies. It is the same ideologies that enable these atrocities. So how are we going to move on from here?” ‘Revolutionaries Never Die,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Concludes the filmmaker: “So there was a real need to reconstruct and re-deal with everything in a way that makes sense somehow. And this film is my answer for this beginning.” Revolutionaries Never Die indeed sees Yaqubi call his cinematic letter to Saab his attempt to “cut through the repetition and disrupt it,” while not losing the belief that you can make films. “It’s this idea of time as a loop, and everything is looping,” he explains to THR . “The same images keep coming again, even inside the same film. So, in my film, I felt that these repeating images, such as some scenes of Jocelyne writing, capture this feeling. Time and space collapse. This is our feeling as filmmakers today. So a chronology of shot after shot doesn’t work anymore.” Revolutionaries Never Die highlights how there was always a positive outlook in Saab’s work. “What is very special about her is that hope she always has,” Yaqubi says. “Even with her house destroyed, she’s like, ‘It’s okay. At least nobody has died. We can continue. We can rebuild. And I think this is the feeling and the sense that I wanted to get across, and I want to project that hope to audiences.” The filmmaker had the title Revolutionaries Never Die from the first minute. “I never changed it,” says Yaqubi. “It comes from [an autobiographical] book of conversations between Palestinian political leader George Habash and French journalist Georges Malbrunot about the revolutionary practices in the Palestinian struggle. My idea was that we always have to keep on making or thinking of revolution, even in the darkest times, because that’s the only way for us not to disappear.” ‘Revolutionaries Never Die,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Concludes the filmmaker: “Jocelyne Saab was a revolutionary not only in the classical sense, but she’s also a revolutionary on a social level. And she is also a revolutionary for being a woman film pioneer. She was a revolutionary in many senses. That makes her — I don’t want to say eternal — but it makes her somebody who never dies. I heard this Arab proverb: You die three times. You die when you die. You die when you’re buried. And the third time you die when nobody remembers you.” THR

title: ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ReelShort On Course To Reach $1BN Revenue & First Profit In 2026 – MPA Report Michelle Yeoh Named As Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Filmmaker Of The Year Warner Bros Korea Sets September Release For ‘The Intern’ Remake, Starring Choi Min-sik & Han So-hee View All August 6, 2026 1:59am ReelShort Founder Joey Jia speaking at APOS Media Partners Asia Microdrama platform ReelShort is on track for a 34% increase in revenue to $1.05BN in 2026, according to a report from Asia-based analytics firm Media Partners Asia . The report, ‘ReelShort/Crazy Maple Studio: Inside the $1BN Micro Drama Machine’, found that ReelShort revenue grew from $97M in 2023 to $400M in 2024 and $785M in 2025. After the bump this year up to just over $1BN, MPA estimates revenue will grow to $1.4BN in 2027 and $1.7BN in 2028. After an estimated $12M net loss in 2025, MPA projects EBITDA of $63M and around $40M of net profit in 2026, rising to $306M of EBITDA at an 18% margin and $225M of net profit by 2028. Related Stories News ReelShort Adapts Cora Reilly's 'Bound By Duty' As Its Latest Mafia Romance Microdrama News Microdrama Audiences Getting Younger & More Male, Holywater Tech Report Finds Looking at the market as a whole, MPA is also predicting that microdrama revenue outside China will grow by 21% CAGR from $3.6BN in 2026 to $9.5BN by 2031. Within that, microdrama revenue in the US will grow from $1.5BN to $3.7BN, while in the Asia Pacific region outside of China it will triple to $2.4BN. Watch on Deadline One reason for ReelShort’s growing revenue and profits is the fact that marketing costs are falling, according to the MPA report. User acquisition and marketing costs are set to decline from 55% of revenue in 2025 to 44% by 2028, a shift worth around $10.5M of EBITDA for every percentage point. MPA said this was due to five factors: hit franchises and their sequels draw a growing share of demand without paid support, and supply much of the advertising creative used to acquire the rest; telco and strategic local market partnerships are adding subscribers at little acquisition cost; more billing is moving to ReelShort’s own web store and direct channels; faster creative testing and a hit rate MPA expects to improve raise the return on each dollar spent; and finally, the paid-social auction is maturing after several years of new entrants bidding up prices. The report also found that consumer payments and subscriptions account for the majority of ReelShort’s business, contribuing around 85-90% of revenue, with subscriptions already making up 60–70% of what viewers pay. Advertising, a small stream before 2024, is predicted to grow to around 15% of revenue by 2028 – and because it pays no app-store commission, roughly 65-70 cents of each advertising dollar flows through to earnings. At the same time, more consumer billing is moving to ReelShort’s own web store, reducing platform and payment fees. Together these two shifts account for close to half of the projected margin expansion. Asia is contributing around 12% of ReelShort revenue in 2026, and is the fastest-growing region in MPA’s forecast, reaching around $200M and 14% of revenue in 2027, with the AIS partnership in Thailand, live since April, delivering significant subscriber and engagement momentum. Latin America and Asia Pacific combined account for around 60% of an estimated 70 million global monthly users in 2026, but only 19% of revenue. North America contributes 59% of revenue with $620M. Narrowing that gap is the main source of upside in MPA’s forecast. MPA concluded the report by saying that microdrama is a five-player market, with ReelShort leading on an estimated 29% share, ahead of DramaBox on 21%, DramaWave on 13%, NetShort on 10% and GoodShort on 6%. The remainder is spread across some 300 smaller apps. “Microdrama has begun to be an earnings story rather than a growth story. Marketing costs are coming down as hit franchises bring audiences in without paid support, platform fees are falling as operators move billing onto their own web stores, and advertising is entering the mix at high margin. ReelShort is showing that the model can scale and make money at the same time. What decides the next phase is distribution and unit economics, not necessarily content volume,” said MPA CEO & Executive Director Vivek Couto. title: Michelle Yeoh Named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at Busan
full_text: Aug 6, 2026 1:26am PT Michelle Yeoh Named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at Busan By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Craig Russell Stars in British Action Thriller ‘The Priest’ as Cornwall Shoot Wraps (EXCLUSIVE) 2 hours ago Michelle Yeoh Named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at Busan 3 hours ago ReelShort on Track for $1.05 Billion Revenue, First Profit at Scale in 2026, Media Partners Asia Report Finds 4 hours ago See All Chen Man Michelle Yeoh has been named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), an annual honor recognizing an Asian film professional or organization for exceptional contributions to the advancement of Asian cinema. Yeoh made her screen debut in Hong Kong action cinema with “Yes, Madam!” in 1985, followed by “Police Story 3: Supercop” in 1992 and “Wing Chun” in 1994, helping redefine what an action heroine could be on screen. She broke through internationally with “Tomorrow Never Dies” in 1997 and “Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon” in 2000, the latter a rare non-English-language title to land both box-office success and critical acclaim worldwide. Her later credits include “Crazy Rich Asians” (2018), “Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings” (2021) and “Wicked” (2024), before her turn in “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022) made her the first Asian performer to claim the Academy Award for lead actress, an awards run that also carried her to victories at both the SAG Awards and the Golden Globes. Earlier this year, she also became the first Asian woman to receive the Honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival. Related Stories France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) Yeoh’s ties to BIFF stretch back to 2002, when she attended the festival for the Pusan Promotion Plan, the precursor to today’s Asian Project Market. She has returned to Busan multiple times since, with screenings including “Far North” (2007), “Reign of Assassins” (2010), “The Lady” (2011), “Master Z: The Ip Man Legacy” (2018), which closed the festival’s 23rd edition, and “Everything Everywhere All at Once” (2022). This year’s appearance marks her first time back on the BIFF red carpet since she attended with “The Lady” in 2011. Popular on Variety BIFF will mark the occasion with a Special Program in Focus featuring three titles Yeoh selected herself: “Reign of Assassins,” “Everything Everywhere All at Once” and “Sandiwara” (2026). Her latest feature, “It’s My Time” (2026), will screen as well, rounding out a retrospective built around her career. The Asian Filmmaker of the Year will be presented during the festival’s opening ceremony, hosted by “Pachinko” star Kim Minha, set for Oct. 6 at Busan’s Cinema Center venue. First established at BIFF’s eighth edition in 2003, the award has previously gone to Jafar Panahi in 2025, Kurosawa Kiyoshi in 2024, Chow Yun Fat in 2023 and Tony Chiu-Wai Leung in 2022. Born in Malaysia in 1962, Yeoh has continued expanding her range on the global stage in recent years, with credits including “A Haunting in Venice” (2023), “Wicked” (2024) and “Star Trek: Section 31” (2025). title: Busan Film Festival to Honor Michelle Yeoh as Asian Filmmaker of the Year
full_text: × Skip to main content By Patrick Brzeski Plus Icon Patrick Brzeski Asia Bureau Chief View All August 6, 2026 12:54am Michelle Yeoh Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images The career honors keep coming for veteran screen star Michelle Yeoh . The Busan International Film Festival revealed Thursday that it has named the Oscar winner its Asian Filmmaker of the Year. Yeoh will accept the honor at the festival’s opening ceremony on Oct. 6 at the landmark Busan Cinema Center. Presented annually since 2003, the award recognizes a film professional or organization for exceptional contributions to Asian cinema — a description the Busan festival said Yeoh has readily fulfilled across her four-decade career in movies. Related Stories Business Soft Ad Market, World Cup Competition Hit Germany's ProSiebenSat.1 Results Movies Locarno Honoree Sigurjón Sighvatsson on AI, Netflix and Why Cannes "Doesn't Know What It Is Anymore" Bursting into Hong Kong’s fabled world of martial arts action cinema with titles like Yes, Madam! (1985), Police Story 3: Supercop and Wing Chun , she helped redefine what women could do in the genre before going global with Tomorrow Never Dies and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon . Her recent Hollywood career — Crazy Rich Asians , Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings , the Wicked films — then culminated with Everything Everywhere All at Once , which made her the first Asian performer to win the best actress Academy Award. The Busan honor will continue a year of career-achievement recognition for Yeoh. In February, she became the first Asian woman to receive the Honorary Golden Bear at the Berlin International Film Festival. Fellow Oscar winner Sean Baker presented her with the award and later premiered Sandiwara , an 11-minute short he wrote, directed and shot on an iPhone in a Penang night market, with Yeoh starring as five intertwining characters. The Anora filmmaker described the film — which was financed by fashion house Self-Portrait —as both a love letter to his star and her native Malaysia. Yeoh has personally curated a three-film program of her work for Busan, comprising Sandiwara , Everything Everywhere All at Once and the 2010 wuxia favorite Reign of Assassins . The festival will also screen It’s My Time , her first Chinese-language feature since the Oscar. Directed by Bai Xue, the crowd-pleasing drama, released in China last month, stars Yeoh as a septuagenarian who discovers a late-life gift for speedcubing, or competitive puzzle-solving. Fresh off her final turn as Madame Morrible in Wicked: For Good , Yeoh will next star in Prime Video’s Blade Runner 2099 . Other recent Busan Filmmaker of the Year honorees have included Jafar Panahi (2025), Kiyoshi Kurosawa (2024), Chow Yun-fat (2023) and Tony Leung Chiu-wai (2022). The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs Oct. 6-15, with Pachinko star Kim Minha hosting the opening ceremony where Yeoh will be feted. THR

title: ReelShort on Track for $1.05 Billion Revenue, First Profit at Scale in 2026, Media Partners Asia Report Finds
full_text: Aug 6, 2026 12:37am PT ReelShort on Track for $1.05 Billion Revenue, First Profit at Scale in 2026, Media Partners Asia Report Finds By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Craig Russell Stars in British Action Thriller ‘The Priest’ as Cornwall Shoot Wraps (EXCLUSIVE) 3 hours ago Michelle Yeoh Named Asian Filmmaker of the Year at Busan 3 hours ago ReelShort on Track for $1.05 Billion Revenue, First Profit at Scale in 2026, Media Partners Asia Report Finds 4 hours ago See All ReelShort Media Partners Asia projects that leading microdrama platform ReelShort will generate $1.05 billion in revenue in 2026, up 34%, and post its first meaningful profit at scale, according to a new report from the Singapore-based research firm. The report, titled “ReelShort / Crazy Maple Studio: Inside the US$1B Micro-Drama Machine,” covers ReelShort’s financial trajectory through 2028 alongside the broader competitive landscape for microdrama outside of China, a category MPA sizes at $3.6 billion this year. Related Stories France’s National Film Board to Reduce Funding for Productions That Fail Gender Equality Targets Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) ReelShort’s revenue climbed from $97 million in 2023 to $400 million in 2024 and $785 million in 2025. After an estimated $12 million net loss last year, MPA projects $63 million of EBITDA and some $40 million of net profit in 2026. The firm expects those figures to keep climbing, with EBITDA reaching $306 million – an 18% margin – and net profit hitting $225 million by 2028, on revenue of $1.4 billion in 2027 and $1.7 billion in 2028. Popular on Variety MPA forecasts outside-China microdrama revenue overall will grow from $2.7 billion in 2025 to $3.6 billion this year and $9.5 billion by 2031, a 21% compound annual growth rate. The U.S. market alone is expected to more than double, from $1.5 billion to $3.7 billion, over that period, while Asia Pacific ex-China is projected to triple to $2.4 billion. A key driver of ReelShort’s improving margins is falling marketing spend. MPA expects user acquisition and marketing costs to shrink as a share of revenue over the forecast period, falling from just over half in 2025 to under 45% by 2028, with each point of decline worth roughly $10.5 million of EBITDA. The firm attributes the trend to five factors: hit franchises and their sequels drawing audiences without paid support and supplying advertising creative; telco and local market partnerships adding subscribers cheaply; more billing shifting to ReelShort’s own web store; improving creative testing and hit rates; and a maturing paid-social ad auction after years of new entrants driving up prices. Consumer payments and subscriptions remain the core of the business, contributing 85% to 90% of revenue across the forecast period, with subscriptions already making up 60% to 70% of viewer spend. Advertising, a minor revenue stream before 2024, is expected to grow to around 15% of revenue by 2028. Because advertising carries no app-store commission, MPA estimates 65 to 70 cents of every ad dollar flows through to earnings. Combined with the shift toward direct billing on ReelShort’s web store, these two trends account for close to half of the company’s projected margin expansion. ReelShort has also been expanding its scripted adaptations, including its recent take on Monica Murphy’s “Things I Wanted to Say” , as part of that content push. Asia is the fastest-growing region in MPA’s forecast, contributing 12% of ReelShort’s revenue in 2026 and rising to around $200 million, or 14% of revenue, in 2027. The company’s partnership with Thailand’s AIS , live since April, has driven significant subscriber and engagement growth. Further telco partnerships in Indonesia and the Philippines are expected to launch by the end of 2026 and contribute for a full year in 2027, while local production and distribution deals in Japan and Korea – including a co-production with Showbox – are set to launch in the fourth quarter. MPA’s data shows a stark mismatch between where ReelShort’s users are and where its money comes from: Latin America and Asia Pacific together make up roughly three in five of an estimated 70 million global monthly users in 2026, yet generate under a fifth of revenue. North America, by contrast, delivers 59% of revenue despite a much smaller slice of the user base. Closing that gap is the main source of upside in MPA’s forecast. MPA counts five major players in the space: ReelShort leads with an estimated 29% share, followed by DramaBox at 21%, DramaWave at 13%, NetShort at 10% and GoodShort at 6%. The remaining share is spread across roughly 300 smaller apps. “Microdrama has begun to be an earnings story rather than a growth story,” said Vivek Couto, CEO and executive director of MPA. “Marketing costs are coming down as hit franchises bring audiences in without paid support, platform fees are falling as operators move billing onto their own web stores, and advertising is entering the mix at high margin. ReelShort is showing that the model can scale and make money at the same time. What decides the next phase is distribution and unit economics, not necessarily content volume.” “User acquisition is the swing factor,” added Myat Pan Phyu, lead analyst for microdrama and vertical video at MPA. “It falls from 55% of revenue in 2025 to 44% by 2028 on our model, and every percentage point is worth around $10.5 million of EBITDA at this year’s scale. The reason is that less of the growth now has to be bought in the paid-social auction. Franchises bring audiences in on their own, and telco distribution adds subscribers at almost no acquisition cost. Thailand has shown that quickly, and the partnerships in Indonesia and the Philippines, along with Japan and Korea from the fourth quarter, should contribute for a full year in 2027.” Founded in 2022 by Crazy Maple Studio, ReelShort has grown into one of the largest vertical entertainment platforms globally, surpassing 286 million downloads and attracting tens of millions of monthly active users, with more than 1,600 staff members and a network of freelance creators and production partners. Founder and CEO Joey Jia has downplayed that download milestone. “Downloads were never our dream or our goal,” he has said . “Our goal is to create diversified content that meets the demands of different audience segments, ultimately serving a wide range of viewers.” A24 Explains Why AI Deal With Google Exists: ‘We’d Rather Have a Seat at the Table Than on the Sidelines’ ‘Obsession’ Sets Peacock Streaming Release Date NBCU’s Peacock Limited-Ads Tier Launches on YouTube Primetime Channels ‘The Five Star Weekend’ Renewed for Season 2 After Becoming Peacock’s Most-Watched Scripted Series Ever Bravo Bucks Tough Ad Trends, Keeping Some Upfront Dollars Moving Away From Traditional Cable (EXCLUSIVE) Olivia Wilde’s ‘The Invite’ Nears $40 Million Globally, Becoming a Rare Hit Summer Comedy Loading comments... title: Soft Ad Market, World Cup Competition Hit Germany’s ProSiebenSat.1 Results
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 12:01am Marco Giordani Courtesy of ProSiebenSat.1 Medien ProSiebenSat.1 posted lower first-half revenue as Germany ‘s weak television advertising market and competition from broadcasters carrying the World Cup weighed on its entertainment business. The German commercial broadcaster, which is controlled by the Berlusconi family’s MediaForEurope (MFE) group , reported first-half revenue of €1.54 billion ($1.77 billion) on Thursday, down 9 per cent from a year earlier. On an organic basis, excluding portfolio changes and currency effects, revenue declined 2 per cent. Second-quarter revenue fell 8.5 per cent to €768 million ($881 million). Related Stories Movies Locarno Honoree Sigurjón Sighvatsson on AI, Netflix and Why Cannes "Doesn't Know What It Is Anymore" Movies Isabella Rossellini Gets Emotional Honoring Her Family Legacy at Locarno's Opening Night The company said advertising revenue continued to be affected by a slowdown in the German TV market, the ongoing shift of ad spending to digital platforms and competition from broadcasters airing major sporting events, particularly the World Cup. Entertainment revenue fell 6 per cent in the first half to €952 million ($1.09 billion), with linear TV advertising down 9 per cent. Digital advertising remained a bright spot. Digital & Smart advertising revenue rose 6 per cent, driven by ProSieben’s streaming service Joyn, content distribution on third-party platforms and the group’s audio business. Advertising-supported streaming revenue at Joyn increased 8 per cent in the first half, while subscription revenue climbed 20 per cent. Despite the revenue decline, earnings improved sharply as the company cut costs and continued a broader restructuring. First-half EBITDA rose by €152 million ($174 million) to €124 million ($142 million), compared with a loss of €28 million ($32 million) a year earlier. Programming expenses fell to €404 million ($464 million) from €496 million ($570 million), while personnel costs declined to €299 million ($343 million) from €416 million ($478 million), reflecting restructuring measures, asset sales and lower content costs. ProSiebenSat.1 has also continued to slim down its portfolio. Since the start of the year, the company has sold six non-core businesses, including Studio71 U.S., as it focuses on its German-speaking entertainment operations. The company is also betting big on Joyn. Last month the streaming service announced a deal with ZDF to add on-demand programming from the German public broadcaster. ProSieben is also developing a shared streaming technology platform with MediaForEurope, for use across the group’s European markets. MFE pan-European network of commercial broadcasters also includes Italy’s Mediaset and Telecinco in Spain. ProSiebenSat.1 reaffirmed its full-year outlook, maintaining its forecast for slight organic revenue growth and a significant increase in EBITDA, while cautioning that visibility in Germany’s advertising market remains limited. title: Edinburgh’s Industry Programme Returns With High-Profile Names & UK Indie Focus
full_text: Skip to main content By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Festival In Focus: Edinburgh Chief Paul Ridd On How The Event Is Becoming A “Legitimate Launchpad” For New & Established Filmmakers Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature ‘Black Lions – Roman Wolves’ & Teases His Next Project On America’s Black Maroons ‘West Side Familia’: Taylor Hosking On Crafting A New West Side Story With Her Feature Debut About Puerto Rican Biker Gang View All August 5, 2026 11:47pm EIFF CEO Paul Ridd and Festival Producer Emma Boa. Credit: Eamonn McCormack. The Edinburgh Film Festival’s industry programme returns this year in an expanded format, centered around a new symposium on the state of independent filmmaking in the UK, aptly titled the UK Film Conference. The festival launched the conference earlier this summer and tapped BFI CEO Ben Roberts as the inaugural keynote speaker. Roberts will take part in an onstage In Conversation session with Picturehouse Creative Director Clare Binns. The conference will run for one day, Saturday, August 15, and was born, Edinburgh director Paul Ridd explains, out of the increasing strength of the festival’s competition strands. “We’re showing work that’s not been seen anywhere else in the world before, which is the driver for industry and press,” Ridd explains, “and if you’ve got those people in town, having a really good moment during the festival to build something where people can talk about the current state and future of independent cinema felt like an opportune moment.” Related Stories News Revealed: The Early-Stage Plans For A New TV Festival In Edinburgh Festivals Christine Vachon, Ewan McGregor & Sarah Brocklehurst Among Names Set For Edinburgh Film Festival's 2026 Industry Programme Alongside the conversation between Roberts and Binns, the UK Film Conference will feature ‘Low Budget, High Ambition’, a session focused on low-budget filmmaking and how UK producers are adapting to an ever-changing landscape. That session will be followed by ‘Would This Get Made?’, an innovative concept that will feature industry professionals being quizzed on how they would approach the production of a range of projects from the past if they came across their desks in 2026. Watch on Deadline “We’ll be asking the speakers, would you make Trainspotting today? Or Four Weddings and a Funeral ?” Ridd says of the unique concept. “It will be a really fun way to look at how these different individuals and organizations think about what their purpose is and what kind of things they’re making now.” Speakers on the panel, hosted by Wendy Mitchell, will include producer Christine Vachon, Stefanie Fahrion (Film4), Alice Ojha (BBC Film), Laura Wilson (Altitude) and Simon Renshaw (Casarotto Ramsay & Associates). The EIFF Industry Talk session ‘New Nightmares’, hosted by horror content creator Chris Mayo (Big Fat Cult ), will conclude the UK Film Conference with speakers discussing the current state of genre filmmaking. Speakers include actor and filmmaker Max Minghella ( The Handmaid’s Tale ) and filmmakers Prano Bailey- Bond ( Censor ), Chee Keong Cheung ( Bad Day at the Office ) and Joby Stephens ( Abandoned ). “In the long term we’re hoping to sort of grow out and build something that potentially feels more open to works in progress or more market premieres,” Ridd says of Edinburgh’s industry offering, which has expanded rapidly since he took the helm in 2023. Ridd is a former acquisitions head at Picturehouse and well-liked among industry folk, which has undoubtedly been useful in attracting high-profile names to the festival. Recent visitors and EIFF industry program participants have included Andrea Arnold, Nia DaCosta, David Hinojosa, and Ken Loach. Beyond the UK Film Conference, high-profile industry guests this year include Ewan McGregor, Bruce Dern, and veteran documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, who will take part in career Q&A sessions, while Kenneth Branagh will be handed the inaugural EIFF Outstanding Contribution to Cinema Award. Burns will arrive in Edinburgh following the UK broadcast of his American Revolution docuseries. The series screened on PBS in the U.S. last November. “We were fortunate in that Ken had already been invited to Edinburgh by the wider International Festival to take part in another event earlier in the month,” Ridd explains. “When we heard that was happening, we jumped at the opportunity to have him at our festival too.” Another early addition Ridd made to the Edinburgh industry lineup was the NFTS Sean Connery Talent Lab. The scheme features 25 filmmakers who are chosen to work on a short project with support from BBC Film. Each team received a £25,000 production budget. The first set of shorts created from the Lab debuted at last year’s festival. This year’s shorts are Bubbles (writer/director Jagoda Tlok); Shutterbug (writer/director Fin Bain); My Little Blue Heart (writer/director Iqbal Mohammed); PANG (writer/director Lara Delmage); St Anthony (writer/director Declan Dineen) and The Angel in the House (writer/director Missy McNaught). Elsewhere, filmmaker Paul Sng will chair an industry talk titled ‘Unmaking the Colonial Gaze in Cinema’ on the generational impacts of colonialism on the moving image. Outgoing BFI Filmmaking Fund Director Mia Bays will chair EIFF’s ‘Business of Film Roadshow’, a session on the filmmaking business, featuring speakers from film financier Head Gear and the law firm Lee & Thompson. EIFF will also once again host its annual session on navigating early career filmmaking with BIFA Springboard. The panel will feature BIFA Springboard alumni, who will discuss their journeys graduating from their first to second feature. The EIFF and the wider Edinburgh Fringe Festival, the Scottish capital’s historic performing arts event, have also continued their partnership for another year. “We’re a completely independent entity, so we run our own business, but we are very invested in partnering and collaborating with Edinburgh institutions like the Fringe,” Ridd says. “We sell tickets through the Fringe app. We work through their channels to promote events, and we find ways to incorporate elements from other programs like hosts from other festivals presenting at our events.” With the EIFF, Fringe Festival, Edinburgh Book, Art and International Festivals, the Scottish capital’s population more than doubles to over one million during the month of August. This year, city officials are prepping for widespread disruptions as Princes Street, the city’s main thoroughfare, will be partially closed following a fire at a former department store. City officials have said their safety and preservation works are expected to take several weeks to complete. Ridd expects minor disruptions to EIFF’s work. “Obviously, these are all things that are outside our control, and when it comes to putting on a large-scale event in the middle of a very busy city at the height of its busyness of the year, everybody’s kind of aware of the challenges that we’re going to face,” he says. “Fortunately, being part of an organization like Festivals Edinburgh, we’re able to get a head start on the plans, but it’s just something people are going to have to factor in as well.” He adds: “I have confidence that we’re going to be able to run an effective and beautiful festival. The 2026 Edinburgh Film Festival will run from August 13 to 19.
